title: Feline Blood Transfusion & Donor Welfare | BHOC Veterinary
description: Feline blood transfusion compatibility, donor sedation and cat blood donation, with ISFM guidance and historical EveryCat and Oxyglobin sources.
heading: Cats are different: blood compatibility and donor welfare.

sections.heading: Feline blood transfusion compatibility
paragraphs: Cats have particular transfusion needs. Their A, B and AB blood types, naturally occurring alloantibodies and additional red-cell antigens make compatibility a clinical concern even before a first transfusion. A mismatched transfusion can be life-threatening. Blood typing and crossmatching matter.

sections.heading: Cat blood donation and donor welfare
paragraphs: Donor welfare matters too. Blood donation places demands on a healthy cat: handling, restraint or sedation, venous access and blood removal. Individual temperament and health therefore matter. Sedation and blood collection each require a clinical risk assessment. Feline donors need careful selection, stress reduction and monitoring before, during and after collection.

sections.heading: Feline blood donor sedation
paragraphs: Feline donation is usually performed under sedation. A 2024 study of 29,201 donation events reported that 95.6% were performed under sedation. Finding a suitable donor and compatible blood takes preparation, time and veterinary resources, especially when a critically ill cat needs urgent support.

sections.heading: Historical Oxyglobin use in cats
paragraphs: EveryCat's Oxyglobin Use in Cats report, published on 17 November 2008, brings together historical experience with a hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier in feline anemia care. It cites a retrospective study of 48 cats, a clinical review and an earlier 72-cat case series. These are historical Oxyglobin publications, rather than new BHOC clinical results.

why: The recipient needs compatible blood. The healthy donor also needs protection. These two responsibilities motivate investigation of additional oxygen-delivery approaches that may reduce dependence on donor animals. Historical Oxyglobin evidence is product-specific and does not establish safety or efficacy for BHOC.
